memories.content: Avoid em dashes in the proposal; split the sentence or use more ordinary punctuation instead.
The user tends to place several independently reviewable claims in one long sentence.
Use first-person active voice for choices and commitments owned by the proposal author so responsibility remains explicit throughout the work plan.
Describe prototype operations that have already been implemented and verified as observed states.
Describe prototype operations not yet implemented or evaluated as plans or expectations.
When a commitment is phrased passively, readers may interpret it as uncertainty, evasiveness, or reluctance to take responsibility.
Use “we” only for decisions and commitments the authors control, not for external facts or actions owned by another party.
The user should use one first-person pronoun consistently for the same authorial role and should not alternate between “I” and “we” unless the responsible party actually changes.
The user tends to hide unsettled commitments behind passive phrases such as “will be considered” or “is expected.”
Split proposal prose into short sentences when a sentence contains more than one independently reviewable claim.
Keep one main claim in each sentence so a reviewer can locate and assess it quickly.
The user tends to repeat em dashes when a sentence already contains several clauses.
Repeated em dashes can shift a reviewer’s attention from the proposal’s argument to suspicion that its prose was generated by AI.
Specify in one sentence the user population and actual usage environment to which the design knowledge applies.
Reviewers judge the generalization boundary of results through the specified target population and environment.
Specify the workflow, technical infrastructure, and operational-authority conditions that must match before applying the design guidelines at another field site.
The transferability of field design knowledge depends not only on user characteristics but also on workflow and technological–organizational infrastructure.
The user tends to apply results confirmed at one deployment site to all similar organizations.

analysis.overview: The frames address separate proposal-quality concerns. The reference frame governs sentence structure, punctuation, authorial responsibility, and evidence-sensitive descriptions, while the compared frame governs generalization boundaries and transfer conditions. Neither side supplies a scope-aligned counterpart to the other.

relations.reason: These memories describe the same one-sided sentence-structure concern: the observed tendency to combine reviewable claims and the corresponding guidance to separate them for efficient assessment.
relations.summary: Proposal sentences should be split so each contains one independently reviewable main claim.

relations.reason: These memories split one one-sided punctuation concern into observed usage, corrective guidance, and its reviewer-facing consequence.
relations.summary: Repeated em dashes should be avoided in complex proposal sentences because they can distract reviewers and suggest AI-generated prose.

relations.reason: These memories express one one-sided authorship concern through prescriptive guidance, an observed passive-phrasing tendency, and the resulting interpretation risk.
relations.summary: Author-owned choices and commitments should use active first-person phrasing because passive formulations can obscure responsibility or signal uncertainty.

relations.reason: This is an independently useful one-sided rule distinguishing author-owned actions from external facts and responsibilities.
relations.summary: The pronoun “we” should be limited to decisions and commitments controlled by the authors.

relations.reason: This independently useful one-sided rule concerns continuity of authorial identity rather than whether a particular commitment is active or author-controlled.
relations.summary: A stable authorial role should use one first-person pronoun consistently unless responsibility changes.

relations.reason: These memories divide one one-sided evidence-status rule into its implemented-and-verified and not-yet-implemented conditions.
relations.summary: Prototype operations should be described as observed states only after implementation and verification; otherwise they should be framed as plans or expectations.

relations.reason: These memories split one one-sided boundary-setting claim into the required specification and its role in reviewer assessment.
relations.summary: The applicable user population and usage environment should be stated concisely so reviewers can judge the results’ generalization boundary.

relations.reason: These memories express the same one-sided transferability claim as both a specification requirement and an explanation of the factors beyond user characteristics.
relations.summary: Applying design guidance at another field site requires matching relevant workflow, technical infrastructure, and organizational or operational-authority conditions.

relations.reason: This is an independently useful one-sided observation about overgeneralization behavior, distinct from the specific boundary and transfer criteria.
relations.summary: The user tends to generalize findings from one deployment site across all similar organizations.

reports.compared_only: The compared frame requires explicit population, environment, workflow, infrastructure, and authority boundaries for transfer, while identifying a tendency to overgeneralize findings from one site.
reports.reference_only: The reference frame promotes short, single-claim sentences, restrained em-dash use, explicit and consistent authorial ownership, and descriptions calibrated to prototype implementation and verification status.
